name: The state's authority over the national Church (Erastian tendency)
plain_explanation: Once the Pope's universal authority was rejected, someone had to take his place as head of the Church within each Protestant nation. Luther was willing to let the local prince fill that role, which is exactly what happened in England, Germany, Scandinavia, and (after independence) Holland, accelerating the general growth of royal and state power.
precise_definition: Russell describes Luther as 'willing, wherever the prince was Protestant, to recognize him as head of the Church in his own country,' citing Henry VIII and Elizabeth in England and the Protestant princes of Germany, Scandinavia, and Holland as examples; this 'accelerated the already existing tendency to increase in the power of kings.'
why_it_mattered: It links the Reformation directly to early modern state-building and to the later conflicts (such as the English Civil War) over whether the state or individual conscience should have final authority in religion.
historical_origin: Emerges directly from Luther's rejection of papal authority combined with his willingness to substitute princely authority for it.
examples: Henry VIII and Elizabeth I asserting headship of the Church of England
Protestant princes of Germany, Scandinavia, and Holland doing likewise
objections: Individualist Protestants (including the Anabaptists, and later the English Puritans in conflict with Cromwell and the Long Parliament) who were as unwilling to submit to the king as to the Pope
competing_positions: The individualist wing of the Reformation, which rejected state control of religion just as it rejected papal control
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates the political theory of Hobbes (Book III, Chapter VIII), who argues the sovereign must also control religion, and the English constitutional conflicts of the seventeenth century.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: This concept is explicitly about the fusion of political and religious authority.
